PAPER: Artificial Intelligence Review (2026) 59:6 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10462-025-11420-6 LIFWCM: local information-based fuzzy weighted C-means algorithm for image segmentation Hanshuai Cui1 · Wenyi Zeng1 · Rong Ma1 · Dong Cheng2 · Qianpeng Chong1 · Zeshui Xu3 Received: 28 October 2024 / Accepted: 30 September 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract Image segmentation aims to partition an image into non-overlapping regions that are co- herent in appearance. Although the fuzzy C-means (FCM) algorithm is widely used for its simplicity and efficiency, it treats each pixel independently and is therefore sensitive to noise. We propose LIFWCM, a local information-based fuzzy weighted C-means algo- rithm that assigns a single-pass, data-driven weight to each pixel by aggregating neigh- borhood intensity variation and positional overlap, and then integrates these weights into the standard FCM objective and a spatially aware membership refinement. This design suppresses the influence of noisy and boundary pixels while preserving details with low computational overhead. Across six experiments on synthetic images and natural images from the Image Processing Toolbox and BSDS500, LIFWCM consistently improves seg- mentation quality under heavy noise. On the BSDS500 image with 30% salt-and-pepper noise, LIFWCM attains 98.96% segmentation accuracy, exceeding the best baseline, and surpassing classical FCM variants. LIFWCM also achieves higher MPA (0.94) and MIoU (0.82) than competing methods, while converging in a few iterations. These results dem- onstrate that LIFWCM is robust to high-intensity noise, preserves fine structures, and remains efficient due to one-time weight computation, making it suitable for real-world noisy images with complex structures. Keywords Image segmentation · Fuzzy C-means algorithm · Clustering algorithm · Local information · Sample weight 1 Introduction Image segmentation is a fundamental technique in computer vision and digital image pro- cessing, involving the division of an image into distinct regions based on its inherent char- acteristics. This process facilitates the extraction of key information for subsequent analysis (Gonzalez et al. 2009). Among various image segmentation methods, clustering-based approaches have been extensively studied. As a classical unsupervised machine learning algorithm, clustering can yield effective results without requiring large labeled datasets. Common clustering algorithms include hierarchical clustering (Zhang et al. 1996; Karypis et al. 1999), grid-based clustering (Bureva et al. 2020; Wang et al. 1997; Sheikholeslami et al. 1998), model-based clustering (Reynolds 2009), partition-based clustering (Mac- Queen 1967), density-based clustering (Ester et al. 1996), and fuzzy clustering (Dunn 1973; Bezdek 1981). Different clustering algorithms exhibit distinct strengths and weaknesses depending on the application context. Fuzzy clustering, in particular, accounts for the mem- bership degree of elements to multiple cluster centers, allowing for varying levels of affilia- tion within each cluster. Consequently, fuzzy clustering aligns more closely with real-world patterns and has been widely adopted. Zadeh founded fuzzy set (FS) theory (Zadeh 1965), which extends the binary values of 0 and 1 to values between 0 and 1, as a powerful tool for describing and dealing with uncer- tainty. The fuzzy C-means (FCM) algorithm, introduced by Dunn (1973) and Bezdek (1981), is a popular research focus because of its efficiency and broad application scope. With the evolution of fuzziness and uncertainty, scholars have recently extended the concept of fuzzy sets to describe fuzziness more accurately. They introduced different types of fuzzy sets and presented several versions of the FCM algorithm. For example, Torra (2010) suggested the hesitant fuzzy set (HFS) in 2010, which considers a set of membership degrees. Zeng et al. (2020) introduced a new image fuzzification and defuzzification method based on HFS, presented the HFCM algorithm, and then employed the algorithm for image segmentation and decision-making. Yager (2013a, b), Yager and Abbasov (2013) examined Pythagorean complement operations, introduced the Pythagorean fuzzy set (PFS), and further refined its operational framework. PFS relaxes the restriction on the sum of membership and non- membership values in a fuzzy set. Ma et al. (2021) presented the PFCM algorithm based on PFS and achieved positive results in the image segmentation task. Many modifications to the FCM algorithm have been introduced to improve the cluster- ing effect, including fusing local information, introducing kernel functions, and improving distance measures. In the image segmentation task, it is efficient to introduce local infor- mation that can mitigate the variation in pixel values and handle noise. Therefore, some FCM algorithm variations that include local information have been introduced recently. For example, Ahmed et al. (2002) developed the FCM_S algorithm, but this algorithm requires additional computation for neighboring terms, resulting in slower execution times. To address this problem, Chen and Zhang (2004) proposed the FCM_S1 and FCM_S2 algorithms that increase the execution speed by modifying neighboring terms. Therefore, FCM_S1 and FCM_S2 are kernel function variations of the FCM_S algorithm. Alterna- tively, Szilágyi et al. (2003) introduced the EnFCM algorithm that uses grayscale values instead of pixels for clustering, leading to faster execution time without compromising seg- mentation performance. Lastly, Cai et al. (2007) combined the strengths of the FCM_S and EnFCM algorithms, resulting in the FGFCM algorithm that integrates both local and grayscale information of the image. The FCM algorithms mentioned above incorporate local information to improve the segmentation effectiveness of noisy images greatly, but they have a common drawback in that they require manual parameter setting. Setting a suitable parameter without knowing the shape, size, and intensity of noise in the image is very difficult. Therefore, FCM algo- rithms that require no parameter tuning are introduced as well. Krinidis and Chatzis (2010) presented the FLICM algorithm. The algorithm effectively preserves image details with- out requiring prior parameter tuning knowledge and demonstrates robustness against noise 1 3 LIFWCM: local information-based fuzzy weighted C-means algorithm for… Page 3 of 30 6 interference. Gong et al. improved the FLICM algorithm and developed the KWFLICM algorithm (Gong et al. 2013). The KWFLICM algorithm modifies the fuzzy factor com- putation method used in FLICM, resulting in a more accurate evaluation of pixel value distribution. Additionally, this algorithm implements the Gaussian kernel function for the similarity measure, which effectively discerns variations among various pixels. However, these two algorithms run slowly due to the additional calculation required for local informa- tion. Memon and Lee (2018) extended the KWFLICM algorithm to work in high-dimen- sional space and presented the GKWFLICM algorithm, which is no longer limited to image segmentation and has a broader range of applications. Some FCM algorithms integrated with advanced technologies have been proposed recently. Using membership filtering and morphological reconstruction, Lei et al. (2018) presented the FRFCM algorithm, which minimizes the computation of local information. Zhang et al. (2019) proposed the DSFCM algorithm, which estimated the theoretical val- ues from the true values and used the estimated theoretical values to cluster. Then, the DSFCM_N algorithm was proposed by the introduction of neighboring information. Jia et al. (2020) presented the RSSFCA algorithm. Chen et al. (2023) introduced the GK-FCM, which improved the clustering performance of ellipsoidal cluster data. Pang et al. (2022) introduced the PR-FCM method, which utilizes the functional relationships between input dataset attributes. Pu et al. (2024) introduced the EM-IFCM algorithm, which modifies edge samples’ weights to improve class separability and convergence. Li et al. (2024) intro- duced the EEDFC model for incomplete time series, which jointly optimizes imputation and clustering. Yu et al. (2024) proposed the FW-S-PFCM algorithm, which addresses the limitations of PFCM by introducing a feature-weight matrix and a suppressed competitive learning strategy. Zhao and Xu (2024) proposed the NFMPAtt-Unet model to address blurry edge regions and improve generalizability in medical image segmentation, achieving supe- rior performance over state-of-the-art models. The standard FCM algorithm fails to incorporate local spatial information, rendering it particularly vulnerable to noise and outliers. While FCM variants that integrate local neigh- borhood information demonstrate some noise suppression capabilities, most still perform inadequately on images with strong noise contamination. In summary, the contributions of this paper are as follows: 1. We introduce a sample weight calculating method that considers the difference between the sample and its neighboring ones to identify potential noise points and assign a small weight. 2. We combine the sample weight into the standard FCM algorithm and propose the local information-based fuzzy weighted C-means (LIFWCM) algorithm, effectively reduc- ing the influence of noisy data on the clustering results. 3. We conduct several experiments to assess the performance of the LIFWCM algorithm in segmenting synthetic and natural images. We also compare its segmentation accu- racy and processing time with eleven other FCM algorithms and the Double-DIP net- work. Experimental results demonstrate that the LIFWCM algorithm achieves robust segmentation performance, even in noisy environments. The remaining sections of this paper are structured as follows. Cui et al. 3 Methodology Images have relative position relationships between pixels, and the standard FCM algorithm treats each sample as independent, thereby failing to make good use of this information. To improve the denoising effectiveness, some FCM algorithms with spatial constraints that require manual adjustment of parameters have been introduced. However, FCM algorithms with local information require considerable computing power to calculate the fuzzy factor representing the local information, and the algorithms take a long time to execute. Inspired by the above algorithms, we propose a sample weight calculation method. As a preprocessor, our approach only needs to calculate the weight of each sample once before the clustering process, and there is almost no additional calculation during the iterative pro- cess. This ensures the segmentation effect while reducing the computational cost. 3.1 Generation of sample weight In this subsection, we introduce the derivation method of the sample weight. To facilitate a clearer understanding of the LIFWCM algorithm and its steps, we have included a flowchart in Fig. 3 that visually represents the entire process. Starting from a grayscale image, we set key parameters and initialize cluster centers. We then perform a one-time local preprocessing to compute per-pixel weights: each pixel’s neighborhood is analyzed to capture local intensity variation and position cues, aggregated into a normalized weight that down-weights noisy and boundary regions. With these fixed weights, the algorithm iteratively updates memberships and centers based on their dis- tances, repeating until convergence or a maximum-iteration limit. Afterward, we apply a spatially aware refinement to the memberships and assign each pixel to its most likely clus- ter to obtain the final segmentation. This design achieves neighborhood consistency with low overhead, stabilizes updates against outliers and boundaries, and improves robustness to heavy noise. LIFWCM formulates a single-pass, data-driven per-pixel weight w i that fuses local intensity dispersion and positional overlap, computed once before clustering and then fixed throughout the optimization. This yields three concrete advantages: (1) Parameter-free local 1 3 LIFWCM: local information-based fuzzy weighted C-means algorithm for… Page 11 of 30 6 Fig. 3 LIFWCM algorithm workflow for image segmentation adaptation: w i is fully determined from local neighborhoods without any user-chosen spatial coefficients, avoiding the tuning burden in FCM S/S1/S2/FGFCM-like models. (2) Iteration- free local term: unlike FLICM/KWFLICM/GKWFLICM, local context is not recomputed within each FCM update; instead, it is injected through w i and one spatially aware member- ship refinement, preserving details while reducing computational cost. (3) Robust weighting of uncertain pixels: noisy and boundary pixels are explicitly down-weighted in both center and membership updates, acting as a built-in robustifier analogous to M-estimation. 3.3 Complexity analysis The LIFWCM algorithm introduces a sample weight calculation method that incorporates local information to reduce the influence of noisy data on clustering results. The time com- plexity of the LIFWCM algorithm is primarily influenced by the computation of sample weights, membership degrees, and clustering centers. The algorithm iteratively updates these parameters, and each iteration involves calculating the weights for each sample based on its neighboring information, which requires O(n k) operations, where n is the num- · ber of samples and k is the number of neighbors. Additionally, updating the membership degrees and clustering centers involves matrix operations, contributing to a time complex- ity of O(n c d), where c is the number of clusters and d is the dimensionality of the data. · · Overall, the time complexity of the LIFWCM algorithm is O(t n (k+c d)), where t is · · · the number of iterations. This makes it slightly more computationally expensive than the standard FCM algorithm due to the additional weight calculation step, but it remains effi- cient for practical applications. In terms of space complexity, the LIFWCM algorithm requires storing the sample weights, membership matrix, and clustering centers. The sample weights and membership matrix each require O(n c) space, while the clustering centers require O(c d) space. Addi- · · tionally, the algorithm needs to store the local neighborhood information for each sample, which adds O(n k) space. Therefore, the total space complexity of the LIFWCM algorithm · is O(n (c+k)+c d). This is comparable to other FCM variants that incorporate local · · 1 3 6 Page 12 of 30 H. Cui et al. information. Therefore, the LIFWCM algorithm’s space requirements are suitable for most image segmentation tasks, especially given its superior performance in noisy environments. 4 Experimental results and analysis We performed multiple image segmentation experiments and compared various evaluation indexes to validate the efficacy of the LIFWCM algorithm. Double-DIP is a framework for image layering. It treats the image processing task as the decomposition of the foreground and background of an image; therefore, it can perform tasks such as image segmentation and denoising. Similar to the FCM algorithm, this method is unsupervised and can extract information from the images for learning. We selected several images from Double-DIP’s website to compare the image segmentation results of the SWFCLIM algo- rithm and Double-DIP. Figure 14 a, d, and g show the original image, Fig. 14b, e, and h show the Double-DIP image segmentation result, and Fig. 14c, f, and i show the LIFWCM image segmentation result (Fig. 14). Remark 10 As shown in Fig. 14, both the Double-DIP and LIFWCM algorithms can seg- ment the objects in the image and achieve good results when segmenting noiseless images. However, the LIFWCM algorithm is better at segmenting the details in the image. For example, for the build image [in Fig. 14 a], Double-DIP does not segment the unmistak- able outline of the building, while the LIFWCM algorithm accomplishes this result. For the Ferris wheel image [in Fig.14 d], the LIFWCM algorithm segmented a sharper frame of the ferris wheel, while Double-DIP only segmented the ferris wheel profile. For the cat image [in Fig. 14g], the LIFWCM algorithm is better for the cat’s details, such as eyes and hair, and Double-DIP incorrectly segments part of the window with the cat. Furthermore, one drawback of Double-DIP that cannot be ignored is that it can only divide images into two classes, i.e., foreground and background. Hence, the application of the Double-DIP in specific scenarios is limited. Remark 11 LIFWCM and Double-DIP are two optimization methods in different directions. For modeling objective, Double-DIP optimizes a reconstruction loss with an exclusion term and task-specific regularization on the mixing mask. It assumes that each latent layer is “simple” in terms of internal patch statistics and that layers are weakly correlated. LIF- WCM minimizes a weighted fuzzy clustering objective on pixel intensities, with per-pixel weights W derived once from local intensity variation and positional overlap, and a final spatial membership refinement. It assumes clusterable intensity structure with spatial coher- ence, and treats noise/boundaries as low-weight contributors. For computational behavior, Double-DIP requires iterative network optimization with image augmentations, often min- utes per image on a GPU. Performance depends on early stopping, noise scheduling, and, at times, coarse “hints” (e.g., saliency or bounding boxes) to resolve layer ambiguities. LIFWCM computes weights once, then performs standard FCM-like iterations with low overhead and fast convergence. It is deterministic given initialization and has no trainable parameters; it runs efficiently on CPU. 1 3 LIFWCM: local information-based fuzzy weighted C-means algorithm for… Page 27 of 30 6 Remark 12 From an optimization perspective, Double-DIP solves a nonconvex inverse problem with a high-capacity generator, balancing multiple losses. Under heavy noise, the reconstruction loss can incentivize fitting noise unless carefully regularized or early- stopped. In contrast, LIFWCM directly embeds a noise-suppression mechanism into the objective through w i, decreasing the influence of inconsistent pixels on both membership and center updates. This is akin to robust M-estimation, where down-weighting outliers sta- bilizes parameter estimates. Furthermore, when segmentation is primarily intensity-driven, the clustering assumption is especially appropriate. Remark 13 Double-DIP can be advantageous in scenarios where the segmentation is not well-explained by simple intensity clusters, and a decomposition into statistically distinct layers better captures the scene. First, when regions share similar grayscale distributions but differ in texture or higher-order patch statistics, DIP priors can separate components based on learned internal recurrence, where intensity-only clustering may fail. Second, Double- DIP is naturally framed for two layers (foreground/background). While one can cascade or extend it to more layers, its sweet spot is binary decomposition with a well-regularized mask. 5 Conclusion We introduce a sample weight calculation method combining local information and propose the local information-based fuzzy weighted C-means (LIFWCM) algorithm. The algorithm calculates a weight for each pixel based on neighboring pixel values and location informa- tion, reflecting the degree of confusion. Then, we evaluated the image segmentation per- formance of the LIFWCM algorithm on synthetic images and public datasets, comparing it with other FCM algorithms. Additionally, we conducted comparative experiments using the neural network-based Double-DIP method. The experimental results demonstrate that the LIFWCM algorithm consistently provides exceptional image segmentation outcomes, even for images with multiple classes and high-intensity noise. The proposed algorithm is optimal when considering both segmentation effects and running time. Future work will focus on several directions. Methodologically, we plan to incorporate adaptive or learned spatial weighting and integrate attention mechanisms. For efficiency and scalability, we aim to optimize GPU/parallel implementations, adopt multi-resolution strate- gies, and design streaming/online variants for large images and real-time scenarios. Finally, we will investigate downstream integration by assessing the impact on subsequent tasks. JSON: Name: lifwcm_seg_pipeline Title: Local information-based fuzzy weighted C-means (LIFWCM) for robust image segmentation of heavily degraded grayscale images Short Hypothesis: Computing a single-pass, data-driven per-pixel weight from local neighborhood intensity variation and positional overlap and incorporating these fixed weights into the fuzzy C-means objective together with a spatial membership refinement will increase segmentation accuracy and region-overlap metrics (MPA and MIoU) on noisy grayscale images compared to standard FCM and existing FCM variants. Related Work: Classical fuzzy C-means (FCM) yields efficient intensity clustering but ignores spatial context and is sensitive to noise and outliers. Spatially constrained variants (FCM_S and derivatives) embed neighborhood terms into the objective to increase robustness but require manually tuned spatial weighting parameters and incur per-iteration neighborhood computation. Approaches that inject local information (FLICM, KWFLICM, GKWFLICM, FGFCM, EnFCM) improve noise handling without explicit global tuning, yet most recompute local factors each iteration, increasing computational cost and slowing convergence. Other recent FCM extensions (FRFCM, DSFCM_N, RSSFCA, PFCM and feature-weighted variants) add advanced regularizers or edge-aware mechanisms but either retain higher per-iteration overhead or introduce additional hyperparameters. Unsupervised deep priors (Double-DIP) can decompose images into layers and denoise, but they are computationally heavy, generally targeted to two-layer decompositions, and may fit noise unless carefully regularized. Across these families the unresolved issues are (1) parameter sensitivity for spatial terms, (2) runtime/iteration overhead when local context is recomputed every iteration, (3) insufficient handling of strong, high-density impulse noise while preserving fine structures and boundaries, and (4) trade-offs between denoising strength and edge/detail preservation. Abstract: This pipeline addresses robust grayscale image segmentation under heavy noise by integrating a one-time, data-driven per-pixel weighting derived from local intensity dispersion and positional overlap into a fuzzy C-means framework. The core idea computes a fixed weight for each sample using a small local window that aggregates neighborhood standard deviation and positional overlap; these weights are injected into the FCM objective and a spatially aware membership refinement, down-weighting noisy and boundary pixels while preserving reliable samples. The primary contributions are (1) a parameter-free, single-pass local weighting scheme that captures local inconsistency and positional relevance, (2) a weighted FCM formulation with spatial membership refinement that uses the precomputed weights without per-iteration neighborhood recomputation, and (3) a concise experimental evaluation demonstrating improved pixel accuracy, region overlap, and faster convergence compared to standard FCM variants. Expected outcomes are substantially higher robustness to salt-and-pepper and Gaussian corruption, improved MIoU/MPA on noisy inputs, and reduced iterative overhead relative to local-information FCM methods. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Synthetic controlled images with known ground-truth regions (multiple shapes) at resolutions 100x100, 250x250 and 300x300. (2) Standard MATLAB Image Processing Toolbox images: 'cameraman' (256x256) and 'screws' (640x480). (3) BSDS500 benchmark: use the 200-image test subset with provided ground-truth boundaries/segmentations (converted to grayscale region maps). (4) Additional natural images used in Double-DIP examples (three representative images) for qualitative comparison. Noise protocols: salt-and-pepper at intensities {0%,5%,10%,20%,30%,35%,40%} and Gaussian additive noise with σ corresponding to 30% dynamic-range corruption; apply independently to each test image. Baselines: standard FCM; spatial-constrained FCM family (FCM_S, FCM_S1, FCM_S2); local-information family (FLICM, KWFLICM, GKWFLICM, EnFCM, FGFCM); recent robust variants (FRFCM, DSFCM_N, RSSFCA, PFCM); and Double-DIP (for binary-layer examples). Evaluation metrics: segmentation accuracy (SA), Mean Pixel Accuracy (MPA), Mean Intersection-over-Union (MIoU), Jaccard Index (JI) and Dice Coefficient (DC) computed on class-labeled pixels; runtime (wall-clock median over 5 runs) and peak RAM; convergence iterations. Implementation and hyperparameters: grayscale inputs; fuzzifier m=2; cluster counts set to known ground-truth c per image (2–4); iter_max=1000; convergence ε=1e-4; default local window 3x3 for weight computation; alternative 5x5 for ablation. Repeats and statistical analysis: run each method with 10 random initializations per image and noise level; report mean±std for each metric; perform paired t-tests (two-sided) comparing LIFWCM to each baseline across images; significance threshold α=0.05. Ablation studies: (A1) remove precomputed weights (equivalent to standard FCM); (A2) recompute the same local-weight formula every iteration instead of single-pass to measure per-iteration benefit; (A3) disable spatial membership refinement to measure its effect; (A4) vary window size {3x3,5x5} and mapping function (tanh vs sigmoid) used to map aggregated local score to [0,1]; (A5) vary cluster count c (over/under segmentation) to evaluate stability. Qualitative comparison: compare segmentation masks and boundary preservation on selected natural images (including Double-DIP examples). Efficiency measurement environment: CPU experiments on a representative workstation (e.g., 3.0 GHz 8-core CPU, 32 GB RAM); report median times. Success criteria: LIFWCM must produce statistically significant improvements (p<0.05) in MPA and MIoU versus standard FCM and majority of FCM variants on noisy conditions (≥30% salt-and-pepper) while matching or improving runtime-overhead relative to methods that recompute local information per iteration. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: (1) Local-weight misclassification: high genuine local variability (textures, high-frequency structures) can produce low weights for valid pixels, causing loss of fine detail or region fragmentation. (2) Thin or low-contrast structures: the 3x3 neighborhood may not capture continuity for very thin objects, leading to under-segmentation. (3) Non-local noise patterns: noise correlated across larger scales or structured artifacts may not be detected by small-window local dispersion and therefore remain influential. Data and evaluation biases: (1) Ground-truth region labels in benchmarks may be inconsistent or coarse, biasing overlap metrics against fine-detail preservation. (2) Using only grayscale intensity ignores color/texture cues, limiting generalization to multi-channel images. Scalability and compute limits: (1) One-time weight computation increases upfront cost and memory for very large images or high-resolution volumetric data; storing per-pixel weights and neighborhood indices may be memory-heavy. (2) While cheaper than per-iteration local recomputation, the method still requires O(n) extra preprocessing time and O(n c) memory for membership storage, which can limit deployment on resource-constrained devices. Limits to generalization: (1) Assumes that meaningful segmentation aligns with intensity clusters; fails for scenes where semantic class separation is primarily texture- or context-driven. (2) The approach is designed for unsupervised grayscale clustering and may require nontrivial adaptation (feature design, color handling, multi-scale aggregation) for varied modalities (color, multispectral, medical imaging). Hyperparameter sensitivity: though parameter-free with respect to spatial weighting coefficients, practical performance depends on neighborhood size and the chosen mapping function (e.g., tanh) and may require dataset-specific tuning for optimal results.
